1. The present claim petition arises out of road accident that occurred on 01.10.2014,
in which the petitioner suffered grievous injury and permanent disability. 
2.  The brief facts of the case are that on 01.10.2014, at about 03:30 PM, petitioner was going along with his friends namely Sumit and Narender Singh on Hero Honda CD Deluxe bearing no. HR-15B-1652, being driven by Narender (who later died in the accident). When they reached near Village Nangura, Kaithal Road, Jind, Haryana, a truck bearing no. GJ-09Y-9479 (hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle) came driven at a high speed, in a rash and negligent manner from the opposite direction Bharat vs Akhilesh on 28 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/51411627/
1 and hit the motorbike on which petitioner was riding. 
Due to the impact, petitioner and his friends fell on the road. While Narender succumbed the injuries and died in the accident, petitioner and his other friend Sumit sustained grievous injuries. 
Petitioner was immediately taken to PGIMS, Rohtak, Haryana and thereafter shifted to AIIMS Trauma Center, Delhi. 
3. On 02.10.2014 an FIR no. 0184/2014 was registered u/s 279/337/338/304A/427 of IPC against the driver of the offending truck. Upon investigation, chargesheet was filed before concerned criminal court. Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA Date:
GUPTA 2024.10.28  04:08:28  +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 2 of 25 ss 4. Respondent no.1 is driver, respondent no.2 is owner of the offending vehicle and respondent no.3 is the insurance company with which such offending vehicle was insured. 
5. In response to the claim petition, respondent no.1 filed his reply denying his fault or negligence in the accident. He pleaded that the petitioner and his two other friends were triple riding a motorcycle and were solely responsible for the accident. It is submitted that the claim filed by the petitioner is exaggerated and further since the offending vehicle was duly insured vide policy no.
1603442334000326 from 13.08.2014 to 12.08.2015, it is the insurance company that is liable to compensate the petitioner.
No reply was filed by respondent no.2 (owner) despite opportunity. 
6. In its reply filed by respondent no.3 (insurance company) it is denied that the accident occurred due to the involvement or rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle. It is pleaded that the petitioner, one of his friend as well as driver of the accidental motorcycle were triple riding in violation of the Traffic Rules and therefore it is the driver of the the motorcycle on which petitioner was a pillion rider, who is solely responsible for the accident. It is further pleaded that since that driver of the motorcycle, owner and insurance company thereof have not been impleaded as a party,
the present claim is bad for non joinder of necessary parties. It is however not denied that the offending truck was duly insured at the time of accident. 
7. After completion of pleadings, following issues were framed on 31.03.2018. 
1. Whether the injured Bharat suffered injuries Digitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.10.28 04:08:33 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 3 of 25 ss in a road traffic accident dated 01.10.2014 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle bearing no.
GJ-09Y-9479 driven by R1, owned by R2 and insured with R3 ? OPP. 
Bharat vs Akhilesh on 28 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/51411627/
2 2. Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP. 
3. Relief.
8. Thereafter, evidence was led on behalf of the petitioner by one Nirmala Hermotia (sister of petitioner), as PW-1.
PW-1 led her evidence by way of affidavit Ex.PW1/A and relied upon her Adhar Card as Ex.PW1/1,
certified copy of the FIR, chargesheet, MLC, RC, Arrest memo, Mechanical inspection report, site plan as Ex.PW1/2 (colly), certified copy of the discharge summary of the petitioner as Ex.PW1/3 (colly), disability certificate of the petitioner as Ex.PW1/4, Bank statement of the petitioner regarding his salary from 08.04.2013 to 05.08.2013 as Ex.PW1/5 and medical bills of the petitioner as Ex.PW1/6 (colly). PW-1 further testified that apart from medical bills, Rs.3 lakhs were spent on hiring of ambulance with life support system for transfer of petitioner to the hospital from time to time. She deposed that expenditure was incurred on special diet of the petitioner also. 
Physiotherapy sessions costed Rs.2000/- per day and such therapy continued for almost 1 years. 
An attendant has been hired who was paid Rs.1000/- per day for 4-5 months. The attendant charges were later reduced to Rs.700/- per day for about 1 year. 
PW-1 was duly cross examined by Ld. Counsel for insurance company. 
9. No further petitioner evidence was led. Respondents also Digitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.10.28 04:08:38 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. 
P.No. 4 of 25 ss chose not to lead any evidence.
10. Final arguments in details were addressed by Ld. Counsel for petitioner and Ld. Counsel for insurance company. It is argued on behalf of petitioner that the petitioner has proved the occurrence of the accident due to rash and negligent driving by the driver of the offending truck. He has proved suffering of grievous injury and permanent physical impairment/ disability of 85% in relation to whole body. It is argued that since the offending vehicle was insured with respondent no.3, such insurance company is liable to compensate the petitioner. 
On the other hand, it is argued on behalf of the insurance company that since it is an admitted fact that the petitioner was triple riding a motorcycle and conducted himself in a way endangering his life and safety, he was solely responsible for the accident. Further, since the owner and insurer of the motorcycle that met with the accident have not been impleaded as parties, the present claim is bad for non joinder. It is further argued that the petitioner has failed to examine himself or any other eye witness to the accident and therefore, his claim cannot be said to have been proved in accordance with law. It is further argued that the driver of the motorbike on which petitioner was a pillion rider,
was also not holding a valid and effective driving licence at the time of accident, insurance company of the offending vehicle cannot be made liable to compensate the petitioner. 
On the basis of pleadings of the parties, evidence adduced and arguments addressed, issue wise findings are as under:

3 CHARU GUPTA Date:
GUPTA 2024.10.28 04:08:43 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. 
P.No. 5 of 25 ss Whether the injured Bharat suffered injuries in a road traffic accident dated 01.10.2014 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle bearing no.
GJ-09Y-9479 driven by R1, owned by R2 and insured with R3 ? OPP. 
11. Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law, proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable. Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & ors. (2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs.
Amir Chand & ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana, 2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken. 
12. In the present case, petitioner has examined his sister as PW-1 wherein she has testified in detail,
the date and manner of accident on the lines of petition. She has categorically deposed that the accident was a head on collision with the offending vehicle which suddenly came from the wrong side of the road from the opposite direction, in a rash and negligent manner. The primary defence raised by Ld. counsel for insurance company is regarding non examination of the injured himself and his plea that the witness examined by the petitioner is not an eye witness to the accident. Even during cross examination, PW-1 has conceded that she was not present at the time of the accident and CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA 2024.10.28 Date:
04:08:47 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 6 of 25 ss that her knowledge about the accident is derived from a person who visited her house to inform her about the hospitalization of her brother. At the same time, it is the plea raised by Ld. Counsel for petitioner that the petitioner has suffered 85% of permanent disability including neurological impairment of his faculties due to which petitioner could not have deposed before the court as a competent witness. This fact is also brought during cross examination of PW-1 wherein she has stated that her brother is still under treatment and is being taken care of by an NGO namely Earth Saviour Foundation. This fact has not been specifically denied by the respondent by putting any suggestion to negate it. This Tribunal has also gone through the disability report of the petitioner which evaluates him with 85% of total permanent physical impairment in relation to the whole body. Though no document regarding specific neurological disability to the extent of disqualifying the petitioner to depose before the court, has been filed, it is observed that in enquiry proceedings under Motor Accident Claim Tribunal Act, strict rules of evidence are not applicable. The petitioner has to prove on the basis of preponderance of probabilities, the occurrence of the accident due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle. To prove such a fact, there is no legal requirement of petitioner being examined, moreso when a chargesheet already stands filed against the driver of the offending vehicle before the criminal Court. In fact, even without examining any witness, mere filing of the Bharat vs Akhilesh on 28 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/51411627/
4 chargesheet against the driver of the offending vehicle and in absence of any defence raised by such driver or the owner of the offending vehicle, is considered sufficient proofDigitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:
2024.10.28 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 7 of 25 ss 04:08:51 +0530 of occurrence of the accident and negligence on the part of the driver of the offending vehicle. As such, the objection raised by the insurance company of not examining the petitioner himself is unsustainable in the present proceedings. 
13. In the present case not only, police (after investigation) had filed chargesheet against respondent no.1 under Section 279/338 of IPC but also the concerned Criminal Court has framed criminal charge u/s 279, 337, 427, 304A & 338 of IPC against respondent no.1 vide its order dated 27.07.2015. Certified copy of such order has been proved vide Ex.PW1/2. The same is strongly suggestive of negligence on the part of respondent no.1 in causing the accident. In National Insurance Co. vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of chargesheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle. 
14. Further neither the driver of the offending vehicle nor its owner have presented any defence by either cross examining PW-1 or by entering the witness box to raise any defence in order to negate or refute the allegations of rash and negligent driving. The involvement of the offending vehicle in causing the accident has not been disputed by either of the respondents. It may further be noted that in Cholamandlam insurance company Ltd. Vs. Kamlesh 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310, it was held that if driver of offending vehicle does not enter the witness box, an adverse inference can be drawn against him. In the present case also, driver did not enter into the witness box to controvert theDigitally claim by CHARU signed CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:
2024.10.28 04:08:56 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 8 of 25 ss of petitioner or even to explain circumstances of accident. 
15. Further, the medical documents i.e. discharge summary Ex.PW1/3 also reveals information that petitioner suffered injuries on account of an accident with a truck. The registration of FIR and admission of the petitioner in the hospital without any inordinate delay and the circumstances,
prove the occurrence of the accident as well as the site plan showing no divider on the road and a head on collision, proves negligence on the part of driver of the offending vehicle. 
16. In totality of circumstances, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the claimant have been able to prove at the scales of preponderance of probabilities that the accident in question, took place due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle bearing no. GJ-09Y-9479 by its driver/respondent no.1 on the date and time of accident. Accordingly, issue no.1 is decided in favour of petitioner/applicant and against the respondents. 
Contributory negligence Bharat vs Akhilesh on 28 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/51411627/
5 17. As regards, the issue of contributory negligence on the part of the petitioner, there is no denial that the petitioner and his two other friends were triple riding their motorbike. PW-1 could not tell if the petitioner was wearing a helmet at the time of the accident. Further, no helmet was recovered from the spot and the criminal record also does not specify that the victim was wearing any helmet. 
It is evident from the facts that the motorcycle that met with the accident was carrying more than one pillion rider, inDigitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.10.28 04:08:59 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 9 of 25 ss clear breach of necessary safety measures (i.e. triple riding). 
It has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Mohd. Siddique vs. National Insurance Company Ltd.
(2020) 3SCC 57 that a pillion rider on a motorcycle along with the driver and one more person on the pillion, may be a violation of law, but by itself cannot lead to a finding of contributory negligence. 
Similarly in the present case, mere triple riding by the victim/petitioner as a pillion rider cannot be considered as contributory negligence. 
Further, as regards the argument of non joinder of owner and insurance company of the motorcycle which the petitioner was riding, it is a settled law that the petitioner is dominus litis of his case. 
Petitioner is at liberty to chose from which of the tort feasors he wish to claim compensation. As such, non impleading of owner or insurance company of the motorbike is not detrimental to the claim petition. 
Issue no. 2 Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP. 
18. In the instant case Insurance company/respondent no. 3 has not raised any statutory defence against respondent no.1 or respondent no.2 and is under the contractual liability arising out of the insurance policy/contract of insurance. As such, respondent no. 3 is liable to compensate the petitioner. 
19. Further it is noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:
2024.10.28 04:09:03 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 10 of 25 ss following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages) 
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
Bharat vs Akhilesh on 28 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/51411627/
6 (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
19.1 In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a) and (iv). 19.2 It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
(v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
19.3. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.10.28 04:09:07 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 11 of 25 ss under Item (ii) (a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence. 
19.4. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof. 
19.5. Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of l u m p s u m a m o u n t s w i t h r e f e r e n c e t o c i r c u m s t a n c e s s u c h a s a g e , n a t u r e o f injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. Decisions of Hon'ble SC and Hon'ble High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary. 19.6. Observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajkumar v. Ajay Kumar & Anr. is quoted hereunder: 
"10. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps. The Tribunal has to first ascertain what activities the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of the permanent ability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life). The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age. The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any Bharat vs Akhilesh on 28 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/51411627/
7 kind of livelihood, or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.10.28 04:09:11 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 12 of 25 ss functions, but could carry on some other or lesser scale of activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood. For example, if the left hand of a claimant is amputated, the permanent physical or functional disablement may be assessed around 60%. If the claimant was a driver or a carpenter, the actual loss of earning capacity may virtually be hundred percent, if he is neither able to drive or do carpentry. On the other hand, if the claimant was a clerk in government service, the loss of his left hand may not result in loss of employment and he may still be continued as a clerk as he could perform his clerical functions; and in that event the loss of earning capacity will not be 100% as in the case of a driver or carpenter, nor 60% which is the actual physical disability, but far less. In fact, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of `loss of future earnings', if the claimant continues in government service, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities as a consequence of losing his hand. Sometimes the injured claimant may be continued in service, but may not found suitable for discharging the duties attached to the post or job which he was earlier holding, on account of his disability, and may therefore be shifted to some other suitable but lesser post with lesser emoluments, in which case there should be a limited award under the head of loss of future earning capacity, taking note of the reduced earning capacity. It may be noted that when compensation is awarded by treating the loss of future earning capacity as 100% (or even anything more than 50%), the need to award compensation separately under the head of loss of amenities or loss of expectation of life may disappear and as a result, only a token or nominal amount may Digitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA 2024.10.28 Date:
04:09:16 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 13 of 25 ss have to be awarded under the head of loss of amenities or loss of expectation of life, as otherwise there may be a duplication in the award of compensation. 
PECUNIARY /SPECIAL DAMAGES (i) Loss of earnings. 
Actual loss of earning:
20. As regards, loss of income, PW-1 has alleged that the petitioner was employed at a salary of Rs.33,000/- per month apart from various other incentives. She has alleged that post accident, injured/petitioner has become 100% disabled and incapacitated Bharat vs Akhilesh on 28 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/51411627/
8 from taking up any job or work. It is submitted that the petitioner has now become completely dependent for his daily chores. Petitioner or PW-1 have however, not filed any document to prove employment or income of the petitioner. Not even any witness such as the alleged employer, has been examined by the petitioner. Petitioner has also not filed any proof of his educational qualification. Considering the same,
notional income of the petitioner, on the basis of his age, can be assessed as that of an unskilled labour as per minimum wages prevailing in Delhi (i.e. address of the petitioner) at the time of the accident. The same were Rs.8554/- per month. 
21. As per the medical records i.e. discharge summary Ex.PW1/3, petitioner was diagnosed with severe head injury (contusion in right temporal lobe with surrounding oedema and a small hematoma in right frontal lobe). He was brought unconscious to the hospital and was also opined to have suffered supracondyler fracture distal femur with intercondyler extension Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:
2024.10.28 04:09:21 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 14 of 25 ss +0530 and proximal tibia fracture (metaphysio diaphyseal). Operative procedure of insertion of ICP sensor and external fixator application for tibia fracture were also performed on the petitioner. Petitioner was admitted on 02.10.2014 and discharged on 26.10.2014. Upon his discharge, his condition reflected in the discharge summary that he was being fed through ryles tube. He was on silcon urinary catheter. 
As such, considering the period of hospitalization, petitioner is entitled to a salary of one month, for the period of hospitalization. Hence, actual loss of income would have Rs.8554/-. 
Loss of future income/earnings:
22. In the present case, petitioner has relied upon a disability certificate issued by VMMC and Safdarjung Hospital dated 13.06.2018 as Ex.PW1/4. As per this certificate, the Medical Board evaluated the petitioner with total permanent physical impairment disability of 85% in relation to whole body. Further, the condition in which the petitioner has been discharged from the hospital and the permanent disability of 85% suffered by him in light of the fact that he has no educational qualification record or special skills, renders him incapable of taking up a job of the nature he was earlier capable of performing. Now, petitioner is not even capable of carrying out his daily chores. In such circumstances, his functional disability is taken to be 100% from the date of accident. 
23. As per Election card of the petitioner filed on record, his age is shown to be 21 years as on 01.01.2005. Thus, petitioner Digitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA 2024.10.28 Date:
Bharat vs Akhilesh on 28 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/51411627/
9 04:09:25 +0530 MACT No: 116/2017 Bharat v. Akhilesh & ors. P.No. 15 of 25 ss would have been around 35 years of age as on date of accident i.e. 01.10.2014. As such, for purpose of calculating loss of future income, a multiplier of 16, as per Sarla Verma judgment, would be applicable in the case and 40% would be added as future prospect as Pranay Sethi judgment. Hence, compensation towards loss of future income is assessed to Rs.8554/- (monthly income) X 12 (annual computation) X 16 (multiplier) + 40% of total income (as future prospect) =Rs.22,99,315/-. 100% of this amount would be Rs.22,99,315/-. Hence so awarded. 
(ii) Future Medical Expenses:
24. Since petitioner has not suffered any amputation, no future medical expense is likely to be incurred on account of artificial limb etc. Thus no compensation can be granted under this head. 
(iii) Expenses relating to treatment:
25. In this case, claimant has proved on record his medical treatment expense/bills (except an invoice no. 3287 issued by Lakshmi Chemists in the name of some Ajay,
invoice no. 24138 issued by Ritik Medicos in the name of some Master Samaksh and a duplicate/copy/repeat bill of invoice no.524 issued by Vimhans Hospital for a sum of Rs.800). The same are to the tune of Rs.1,14,948/- and accordingly, awarded as expenses towards medical treatment.
Apart from expenditure on treatment, a sum of Rs.50,000/- is granted for conveyance, Rs.50,000/-
on special diet and Rs.5,00,000/- (five lakhs) as cost of nursing/ attendant.
